one_liner: 2009 gist: HotSpot Java 6 runs an alternating two-class virtual-call loop 2.3x faster than 32-bit g++ 4.0.1 -O3.
what_it_does: A results gist (hipertracker, 30 March 2009) for a 30-40 line microbenchmark written in C++ (gist 87516), Java (gist 87518) and Scala (gist 87760): struct/class A has a virtual perform() that adds 1 to a global static int, B overrides it to add 4, and bench() calls perform() 400 million times through a base pointer chosen by (i & 1) == 0 ? a : b, printing the elapsed milliseconds. It is a demonstration, not a library; the only thing to reuse is the observation about how each runtime handles a two-target polymorphic call site.
how_it_is_fast: The author gives no mechanism. The likely one is HotSpot's profile-guided bimorphic inlining: the call site's type profile records exactly two receiver classes, so C2 compiles a class check plus both inlined perform() bodies instead of a virtual call. g++ 4.0.1 has no devirtualization or profile feedback here, so each iteration is a real indirect call through the vtable, in a 32-bit i686 build that passes this on the stack. Derived from page data: about 11.6 cycles per iteration for C++ (1651.8 ms / 400M at 2.8 GHz) against about 5 cycles for Java at steady state (716 ms).
when_to_use: As a minimal, easy-to-read demonstration that a JIT with type profiles can beat an ahead-of-time indirect call at a hot call site that sees exactly two receiver types.

When arguing whether to move hot polymorphic Java code to C++ through JNI: a plain C++ virtual call without devirtualization can lose to HotSpot's inlined dispatch, so a port needs templates, final classes, a type switch or PGO to pay off.
As a starting point for a modern re-run (current GCC or Clang at -O2/-O3, with and without -fprofile-use, 64-bit target, against a current JDK) before quoting any ratio.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Java beats current C++: the C++ side is Apple g++ 4.0.1 (2005-era compiler) building 32-bit code tuned with -march=pentium4 for a Xeon, against a 64-bit HotSpot VM, and no modern compiler, PGO or LTO build was measured.
For megamorphic call sites (three or more receiver types), where HotSpot falls back to a vtable or itable call and the inlining advantage this loop shows does not apply.
For short-lived processes or code that runs once: the first two Java iterations took 967 and 1036 ms (1015 and 955 ms in the gist's first revision) before settling around 716-769 ms.
For C++ code that can already avoid the indirect call (templates or CRTP, std::variant with std::visit, final classes, or a manual type switch); those were not measured here.
As a general language comparison: one call site, a global counter update as the only work, no memory traffic beyond that counter, and one author's single run per variant.

integration.form: source-drop (three short gists: C++ 87516, Java 87518, Scala 87760)
integration.dependencies: none (C++ <ctime> and <iostream>; Java SE 6; Scala 2.7.3 library for the Scala variant)
integration.min_toolchain: as published: Apple g++ 4.0.1 (build 5493), Java 1.6.0_07, Scala 2.7.3; any C++98 compiler and JDK 6+ should build it
integration.platforms: measured on Mac OS X (darwin9) on 2x 2.8 GHz Xeon, 8 cores; C++ built 32-bit (i686) and Java run on the 64-bit HotSpot Server VM

gotchas: The published C++ source does not match the posted numbers: gist 87516 went from four bench() calls (29 March) to a 10-iteration loop and then, in its latest revision, five bench() lines that the page shows without semicolons, while the results gist lists ten C++ timings in one block from its first revision. The ten numbers most likely come from one run of the 10-iteration revision, not from two runs of the five-call version as the verifier assumed; the kernel (400M-iteration loop, A/B classes, (i & 1) alternation, clock() timing) never changed.

The Java command line was edited after the measurement: revision 5 of the results gist posted the 967/1036/769/... numbers under 'java Bench -J-Server', which passes '-J-Server' to Bench.main as an ignored program argument rather than to the VM, and a later revision only relabelled it 'java -server Bench'. The effect is cosmetic because the reported VM is the 64-bit HotSpot Server VM and the first revision's plain 'java Bench' run (1015, 955, then 716-754 ms) shows the same steady state.

The C++ counter is a signed 'static int' that receives 1,000,000,000 per bench() call, so it overflows INT_MAX during the third call, which is undefined behaviour in C++ (Java's int wraps by definition); the printed final count is meaningless and is not a cross-language checksum, though the overflow is unlikely to have changed the timing.

C++ is timed with clock() (process CPU time) and Java with System.currentTimeMillis() (wall time, which includes JIT compilation during the first iterations); 'PowerMac' in the hardware line is presumably an Intel Mac Pro, since the gcc target is i686-apple-darwin9, and the CPU model is not stated.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Prefer the LangArena and benchLANG HotSpot entries (GCC 16 and Clang 22 baselines, many C/C++ configurations) or xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c for current evidence; pick this gist only as the smallest isolated example of a JIT's bimorphic inlining beating an un-devirtualized C++ virtual call.
verified_claims_summary: On a 2x 2.8 GHz Xeon Mac (8 cores, Mac OS X 10.5), 400 million alternating virtual calls took 1651.8-1796.2 ms in C++ built by Apple g++ 4.0.1 -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -march=pentium4 (32-bit i686) against 716-1036 ms in Java 1.6.0_07 on the 64-bit HotSpot Server VM (716-717 ms after warm-up), so about 2.3x faster at steady state and 1.7x on the first Java run (derived from page data); Scala 2.7.3 on the same JVM reached 716-717 ms.
status_note: Abandoned since 30 March 2009, no license, reference-only; the code is trivial to re-run, and any use of the 2.3x figure should be preceded by a re-measurement with a current 64-bit GCC or Clang build (ideally with and without PGO).
